name: Raft ReadIndex & Lease-Read Linearizability
tagline: Serving linearizable reads without writing to the Raft WAL—comparing ReadIndex quorum heartbeats against bounded Lease Reads.
purpose: Understand why reading directly from a Raft leader's local memory can return stale data during a partition, and how ReadIndex and Lease Read preserve linearizability at 10x–100x higher read throughput.

prerequisites.title: Raft Consensus & Leader Election
prerequisites.summary: Know how Raft commits log entries via majority quorum and why an isolated leader can stay unaware of a new term.

prerequisites.title: Monotonic Clocks & Clock Drift
prerequisites.summary: Understand that NTP wall clocks can jump backward, whereas `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` advances steadily within bounded hardware drift.

spark.summary: ReadIndex avoids Raft WAL writes by confirming leadership via a lightweight heartbeat quorum and waiting for `applyIndex >= commitIndex`, while Lease Read serves reads locally in <1 ms using a bounded monotonic leader lease.
spark.keyTakeaway: When serving linearizable reads from a Raft cluster without burning WAL disk I/O, use ReadIndex for clock-independent safety or Lease Reads when monotonic clock drift is strictly bounded below the election timeout.
spark.byteSummary:
A common misconception is that reading from the Raft Leader's local state machine is automatically linearizable. If the Leader gets network-partitioned from the majority, the other nodes elect a new Leader and commit newer writes—while the isolated old Leader still thinks it is Leader and serves stale data!

To prevent stale reads without appending dummy `No-Op` entries to the Raft WAL, etcd and TiKV use **ReadIndex**: (1) the Leader records `readIndex = commitIndex`; (2) it sends a lightweight heartbeat round to Followers and waits for a majority quorum ack (proving no newer Leader exists); (3) it waits until `applyIndex >= readIndex`; and (4) serves the read from memory—zero disk `fsync` required.

For sub-millisecond reads without even a heartbeat RTT, **Lease Read** lets the Leader serve reads locally as long as its monotonic lease (`last_quorum_ack + election_timeout / max_drift`) has not expired. If a GC pause or VM live-migration stalls the clock beyond the drift bound, Lease Read can briefly violate linearizability—making ReadIndex the safer default across public clouds.

learningJourney.title: P · Problem & The Deposed Zombie Leader Trap
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Proves why naive local leader reads violate linearizability during asymmetric partitions.

explanation.foundation: Suppose Node A is Leader of a 5-node Raft cluster (`term 1`, `x = 1`). A network partition isolates Node A from Nodes B, C, D, E.
explanation.core: Nodes B–E elect Node B as the new Leader (`term 2`) and commit `x = 2`. Meanwhile, Node A has not yet received any higher-term message, so it still believes it is Leader! Any client still connected to Node A that reads `x` locally gets `x = 1`—a stale read after `x = 2` was already committed.
explanation.deepDive: Appending every read to the Raft log (`LogRead`) fixes this, but forces disk `fsync` and network replication on every single `GET`—capping read throughput at write throughput.

learningJourney.title: R · Representation: The 4-Step ReadIndex Protocol
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Shows how ReadIndex proves leadership and catches up the state machine without touching disk.

explanation.foundation: ReadIndex separates *proving you are still Leader* from *writing to disk*.
explanation.core: Step 1: Leader captures `readIndex = commitIndex` (and ensures it has committed at least one entry in its current term!). Step 2: Leader broadcasts a heartbeat with an incremental `readCtx` and waits for `floor(N/2) + 1` acks. Step 3: Leader waits until its local `applyIndex >= readIndex`. Step 4: Leader reads its local state machine and replies.
explanation.deepDive: Follower Read Offload: Followers can ALSO serve linearizable reads! A Follower asks the Leader for `readIndex`, waits until the Follower's own `applyIndex >= readIndex`, and serves the read locally—scaling read throughput horizontally across all N nodes.

sectionDiagram.title: Client -> Leader (Record commitIndex) -> Quorum Heartbeat -> Apply Wait -> Reply

learningJourney.title: I · Invariant: Bounded Monotonic Clock Lease Reads
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Explains how Lease Reads eliminate the heartbeat RTT and the exact clock-drift safety condition.

explanation.foundation: In Raft, Followers cannot start an election until `election_timeout` has elapsed since the Leader's last heartbeat.
explanation.core: If the Leader receives a majority quorum of heartbeat acks starting at `t_start`, no new Leader can be elected before `t_start + election_timeout / max_clock_drift`. Until that local monotonic deadline expires, the Leader can serve linearizable reads in <1 ms with zero network messages!
explanation.deepDive: Once `now > lease_expiry`, the Leader refuses local lease reads and falls back to `ReadIndex` until the next heartbeat quorum renews the lease.

learningJourney.title: M · Mechanics at Scale: ReadIndex Batching & Term-Commit Rule
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Shows how batching ReadIndex heartbeats serves 100K RPS and why newly elected leaders must commit a No-Op first.

explanation.foundation: Under 100K RPS reads, sending 100,000 separate ReadIndex heartbeats per second would flood Followers.
explanation.core: Batch all concurrent ReadIndex requests arriving within a 1–2 ms window onto a **single** quorum heartbeat! One heartbeat proves leadership for all 200 waiting reads at once. Also, a brand-new Leader MUST commit a `No-Op` entry in its new term before serving ReadIndex, because Raft's `commitIndex` isn't guaranteed up-to-date until a current-term entry commits.
explanation.deepDive: In `etcd`, `ReadIndex` batching keeps read latency around 1–2 ms intra-AZ while remaining 100% immune to clock skew or VM pauses.

decisionFramework.problem: How to scale linearizable Raft reads without WAL disk overhead or stale zombie-leader reads.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Serve reads directly from Leader RAM without checks, or append every read to the Raft WAL.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Unchecked local reads return stale data during partitions; WAL-logged reads cap read QPS at disk fsync speed.
decisionFramework.alternatives: LogRead vs. Batched ReadIndex vs. Monotonic Lease Read.
decisionFramework.decision: Default to Batched ReadIndex (plus Follower ReadIndex offload) in cloud VMs; enable Lease Read only when hardware monotonic clocks and GC pauses are strictly bounded.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: ReadIndex pays ~1 intra-AZ heartbeat RTT (amortized across batches) in exchange for zero reliance on physical clock accuracy.

learningJourney.title: E · Edge Cases, Assumptions & When NOT to Use Lease Reads
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Highlights VM live-migration, GC pauses, and when stale follower reads are cheaper.

explanation.foundation: Lease Reads depend on a physical time assumption: that the Leader's monotonic clock advances at roughly the same rate as Followers' election timers.
explanation.core: When NOT to use Lease Reads: on garbage-collected runtimes with multi-second Stop-The-World pauses (e.g., un-tuned JVM) or cloud VMs subject to silent hypervisor live-migration pauses (>500 ms freeze). During a 2-second freeze, the Leader's monotonic clock can still appear valid locally right after wake-up while Followers already elected a new Leader!
explanation.deepDive: Assumptions & Limitations: ReadIndex assumes majority quorum availability (fails during minority partition, which is required by CAP/CP linearizability). If a caller only needs eventual/bounded-staleness config reads, serve `serializable` reads directly from any Follower with zero quorum check. Glossary: Linearizability (every read sees the latest completed write in global real-time order), `commitIndex` (highest log entry replicated to a majority), `applyIndex` (highest entry applied to the state machine), No-Op Entry (empty log entry committed upon leader election).

decisionExercise.prompt: Your 5-node Raft cluster runs on cloud VMs using Lease Reads (`election_timeout = 1.0s`, `lease = 0.8s`). A hypervisor live-migrates the Leader VM, freezing its CPU for 1.5 seconds. Why is Lease Read dangerous here?

options.label: Followers time out after 1.0s and elect a new Leader, while the migrated old Leader may serve stale Lease Reads if its clock or timer lags behind.
options.explanation: Correct! VM freezes and STW GC pauses break the bounded-clock-drift assumption of Lease Reads; Batched ReadIndex remains linearizable.

options.label: VM migration corrupts the Raft WAL checksums.
options.explanation: Live migration pauses execution; it doesn't corrupt disk checksums.

options.label: Followers automatically pause their election timers during Leader VM migration.
options.explanation: Followers cannot distinguish a VM pause from a crashed Leader.

steps.explanation: Leader's monotonic lease is valid; it reads its state machine locally in 0.4 ms.

steps.explanation: Lease expired; Leader batches 120 waiting reads onto one heartbeat and gets 3/5 quorum acks.

steps.explanation: Deposed Leader fails quorum heartbeat and refuses to serve stale reads, preserving linearizability.

steps.title: New Leader Commits No-Op & Serves
steps.explanation: New Leader commits a No-Op in term 2 and resumes linearizable ReadIndex/Lease service.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why can reading directly from a Raft Leader's local memory without ReadIndex or Lease Read return stale data?

options.text: An isolated old Leader may not know a majority already elected a new Leader and committed newer writes.
options.feedback: Correct! Without a quorum heartbeat or active lease, an old Leader cannot prove it hasn't been deposed.

options.text: Because Raft Leaders never apply committed entries to their state machine.
Because Followers overwrite the Leader's WAL during reads.
options.feedback: Followers never overwrite a higher-term Leader's WAL.

options.text: Because Raft uses UDP instead of TCP.
options.feedback: The zombie-leader issue is fundamental to asynchronous networks, regardless of TCP/UDP.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Linearizability requires confirming leadership via quorum (ReadIndex) or bounded time (Lease Read).

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must a newly elected Raft Leader commit at least one entry (a `No-Op`) in its current term before serving `ReadIndex`?

options.text: Because in Raft, `commitIndex` from a prior term is not guaranteed to be up-to-date until a current-term entry is committed.
options.feedback: Correct! Committing a current-term No-Op advances `commitIndex` to include all prior committed entries.

options.text: To reset all Followers' monotonic clocks.
options.feedback: ReadIndex does not rely on Follower clocks.

options.text: To delete old snapshots from disk.
options.feedback: No-Op entries do not trigger snapshot deletion.

options.text: To switch from Leader to Follower.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Raft's Figure 8 safety rule requires committing a current-term entry before `commitIndex` reflects all committed state.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should a Lease Read timer start from when the Leader *sent* the heartbeat rather than when it *received* the quorum acks?

options.text: Because Followers' election timers reset when they receive the heartbeat (at or after `send_ts`), so bounding from `send_ts` is strictly conservative.
options.feedback: Correct! Network RTT delays mean `receive_ts` is later than `send_ts`, which could overestimate remaining lease time.

options.text: To make the lease last 10x longer than `election_timeout`.
options.feedback: The lease must be strictly shorter than `election_timeout`.
Lease timing is orthogonal to ReadIndex batching.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Using `send_ts` guarantees the Leader's lease expires before any Follower's election timeout can fire.

beginner.summary: Raft ReadIndex and Lease Reads let a cluster serve fast linearizable reads from memory without writing every read to disk.
beginner.keyTakeaway: When serving linearizable reads in Raft, use ReadIndex heartbeats or bounded Lease Reads instead of writing reads to the WAL.
beginner.byteSummary: An isolated old Raft leader can accidentally serve stale data. ReadIndex checks with a majority via a quick heartbeat, while Lease Reads use a short timer so reads finish in <1 ms.

intermediate.summary: ReadIndex records `commitIndex`, confirms quorum via batched heartbeats, and waits for `applyIndex >= readIndex`; Lease Read skips the RTT using bounded monotonic leases.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: When scaling Raft reads, batch ReadIndex heartbeats (or offload to Followers) for clock-free safety, and use Lease Reads only with bounded clock drift.
intermediate.byteSummary: Batched ReadIndex achieves 100K+ RPS without WAL fsyncs or clock assumptions; Lease Reads cut latency to <1 ms when monotonic drift and GC/VM pauses are bounded.

advanced.summary: Leader term No-Op commitment, 1 ms ReadIndex heartbeat batching, Follower ReadIndex offload, and `send_ts`-anchored monotonic Lease Reads.
advanced.keyTakeaway: When operating Raft in cloud VMs with possible hypervisor pauses, prefer Batched ReadIndex + Follower offload over Lease Reads to guarantee strict linearizability.
advanced.byteSummary: Committing a term No-Op, batching ReadIndex heartbeats, and anchoring Lease Read bounds to heartbeat `send_ts` protects linearizability—while avoiding Lease Reads under STW GC or VM live migration.
